issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette:
Rajesh, a 53-year-old painter originally from a small town in Gujarat, had spent the last fifteen years building a quiet life in a suburban American city with his wife. His work was his identity-the steady hand, the eye for color, the satisfaction of transforming a blank wall into something whole. He had never imagined that a four-month period back in his home region, visiting family during a period of civil unrest, would dismantle everything he understood about himself. It happened on a Tuesday afternoon. He was walking to a local market for vegetables when a mortar shell struck the intersection two blocks ahead. The sound was not a bang but a tearing, a pressure that seemed to split the air itself. He threw himself behind a parked rickshaw, and in that moment, his body locked into a tight curl-knees to chest, arms over his head, spine braced against the vibration of the ground. When the dust settled, he saw parts of bodies he could not name, and the smell-acrid smoke, burning rubber, and something metallic and sweet that he later learned was blood-filled his nose and throat and would not leave. He spent the next three hours in a daze, helping strangers carry the wounded, until a neighbor found him and took him home. He left the region within the week, telling himself he was fine.

Back in the States, Rajesh returned to work within a month, but something had shifted. He began to notice that ordinary sounds-a car backfiring, a child dropping a metal tray in a restaurant-made him jump so violently that his coffee would spill, his heart hammering against his ribs for minutes afterward. He started keeping his body tense without meaning to, his shoulders hunched, his jaw clenched, as if waiting for the next explosion. He found himself scanning parking lots and street corners, cataloging possible cover, and he was ashamed of it. He had never been a fearful man. What frightened him most was the feeling that his own body had become a traitor, perpetually coiled and ready, even when his mind knew there was no danger.

The smells were worse. The scent of grilled meat at a summer barbecue would stop him mid-sentence, because it carried the undertone of that sweet metallic smell. He would excuse himself and stand in the bathroom, breathing through his mouth, until the wave passed. He began to avoid the news entirely, turning off the television when reports mentioned conflict anywhere in the world. He could not bear the footage, the familiar rubble, the sound of sirens. When his wife asked why, he said it was too depressing, but the real reason was that the images made the memory feel as if it were happening again, and the memory itself had become something he could not trust. When he recalled that afternoon, parts of it felt like a movie he had watched, not a life he had lived. He would think, This cannot have happened to me, even as his body would curl into that same tight ball on the couch, knees to chest, arms over his head, while his wife watched in alarm.

He started working longer hours, taking on jobs he would have turned down before, not because he needed the money, but because being busy kept the thoughts at bay. When he was painting, he could focus on the brushstroke, the drying time, the clean line. But the moment he stopped, the questions would return. He would lie awake at night, going over and over the same ground: Why did I go to that market that day? Why did I survive when others did not? What was the point of it? He had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. The work that had once defined him now felt hollow. He was no longer capable of the steady concentration his craft required; his hand would tremble on the ladder, and he would have to come down. The world, he was certain now, was a dangerous place, and he could not protect himself or his wife from it.

His wife noticed him withdrawing. He stopped suggesting weekend outings. He stopped laughing at her jokes. She found him one night sitting in the dark garage, staring at a wall he had primer-coated that morning. When she asked what was wrong, he said, "I don't know who I am anymore." That was when she insisted he call a therapist. Rajesh came to the first session with his hands folded in his lap, the posture of a man who had been carrying something heavy for a long time. He said he did not know if talking would help, but he was tired of being afraid of his own life. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to feel like himself again-to wake up and not already be bracing for the next explosion.
